summary:
Mission Control: Moon is a 3D browser game that lets students aged 10+ design, fly and complete a full Apollo 11 mission, from concept to splashdown, using real numbers from NASA mission records.

Players manage a budget, choose and stack a Saturn V, load fuel and oxidizer for every stage, pick the crew, spacecraft and suits, then fly it: launch and staging, a parking orbit, the TLI burn, braking into lunar orbit on a figure-8 free-return path, landing, a moonwalk with rovers and science, and re-entry through a 2,760 °C heat shield to splashdown.

It addresses the challenge by showing how choices connect as one system: a heavier rocket costs more, too little braking sends you home, a parachute on the Moon crashes you. Every failure explains why, so players learn by trying again.

It matters because ideas like “gravity is everywhere; orbits are free fall” and Kepler’s laws are hard to learn from textbooks. Here, players feel them. Our physical PROMISE rover prototype, with a soil-moisture sensor, links the game to real hardware and to Artemis-era water hunting.
details:
What it does and how it works

Mission Control: Moon is a single-player (1–4 player setup) 3D browser game that walks students through a complete lunar mission, in four parts:

  1. Design: The player gets a $2B budget, with an optional $1B loan at 15% interest. They choose a mission path (free return) and a landing site, buy and stack a Saturn V, and fuel each stage, picking the right fuel and remembering the oxidizer. Then they choose the crew, build the Command and Lunar Modules, add safety systems (escape tower, water deluge), pick a launch window and assemble Artemis-style spacesuits. A live weight matrix and budget show the consequences of every choice.
    • planting the flag, with myth-busting about why it seems to wave;
    • building and driving the Moon buggy;
    • collecting rocks and a special “Genesis” rock;
    • deploying our PROMISE rover to find water ice;
    • setting up the laser mirror and the seismometer.
  2. Home: Ascent, docking, crew and rock transfer, jettisoning the ascent stage, the TEI burn, the speed-up on the way back to Earth, CM/SM separation, re-entry (2,760 °C heat shield, radio blackout), drogue and main parachutes, and splashdown.

A Training Academy offers short lessons and badges on orbits, staging, TLI, docking, landing and spacesuits. A 🎬 Demo mode shows the whole flow quickly.

Benefits and intended impact

  • Systems thinking: players see how mass, money, fuel and timing affect each other, which is the core of real mission design.
  • Learning by failing safely: every mistake explains the physics behind it, with simple language written for a 12-year-old.
  • Correcting misconceptions: “there’s no gravity in space” (orbits are free fall), “the landing was faked” (no air means no parachute, a flag rod, permanent footprints, a 2.6 s radio delay).
  • Who it is for: students aged 10+, classrooms and families. The aim is to spark interest in STEM and in the Artemis program among the generation that will build the first lunar base.

Tools and technologies

  • Software:
    • HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with three.js (r128) for 3D.
    • The browser’s Web Audio API for sound and the Speech Synthesis API for voices.
    • It runs in any modern browser with no installation and can be hosted on GitHub Pages.
  • Hardware: the PROMISE rover prototype, a 4-wheel rover built on an Arduino UNO R4 Minima with 4 TT gear motors and an L298N motor driver, and a soil-moisture sensor for water detection.
  • Data: published NASA mission numbers (Apollo 11 Mission Report and Press Kit, the NASA Moon Fact Sheet, Lunar Laser Ranging, LCROSS, Apollo 15). Sources are listed in the GitHub README.
  • AI: Claude (Anthropic) helped write most of the code from my design and feedback, and helped check facts and write text. All design decisions, testing, the hardware build and the final review are mine.

Creativity

  • One continuous mission: it connects design, flight, surface work and the return in one story, where most tools teach rockets or orbits in isolation.
  • Mixed 2D and 3D: the 2D orbit view makes orbital mechanics clear, and the 3D scenes give the “being there” feeling.
  • Myth-busting through play: players don’t take our word for it; they see the physics.
  • Game linked to hardware: the in-game PROMISE rover matches a working physical prototype.
  • Real Apollo 11 numbers, set in 2026: real launch windows, with Artemis-style suits.

Factors considered

  • Accuracy vs. playability: real values are rounded or scaled where needed (for example, orbit sizes), and this is stated in the game.
  • Age-appropriate language and pacing: fun first, with deeper explanations kept in optional 💡 buttons so they don’t interrupt the flow.
  • Accessibility: it runs in the browser on ordinary laptops, with no installs.
  • Short attention spans: quick feedback, points, lifelines and celebrations from Mission Control.
  • Honesty: PROMISE is our own concept name, not a NASA mission. The AI use is disclosed.
